subsection: 1. Processed foods and three processed-food profiles

notes.b: A processed food is any food changed from its raw state by one or more processes, such as milling, heating, freezing, drying, canning or adding ingredients. Processing makes a raw food safer, longer-lasting, more convenient or more valuable.
points: Main reasons for processing: to extend shelf life, make food safe to eat, cut down on waste, provide a wide choice of good-quality food all year round and create new food products, which varies the diet.
The range of processed foods includes frozen, canned, dried, instant or ready-to-eat and cook-chill foods, as well as preserved or pickled foods and fortified foods.
Minimal processing includes washing, cutting, bagging salad leaves or freezing vegetables, with no ingredient added, so the food stays close to its raw state.
Extensive processing involves many stages and ingredients, so the finished product is far removed from its raw material.
notes.tip: If asked to give two reasons for processing, pick two clear ones, such as extending shelf life and making food safe. If asked to outline the range of processed foods, name categories and give an example of each.

notes.b: Flour is the standard example of extensive processing: wheat grain is turned into a fine powder that looks and behaves nothing like the raw grain, and it then becomes the base of many other foods.
points: Flour is made by cleaning and blending wheat grain, then milling it between rollers (break rolls and smooth rolls) and sieving it. This separates the bran and germ from the starchy endosperm (the white inner part of the grain), and white flour is mainly endosperm.

Removing the bran and germ lowers fibre and some vitamins and minerals, so white flour has fewer of these than wholemeal flour. Nutrients lost in milling, for example B vitamins and iron, may be added back, and flour is a food named as fortified.
White flour keeps longer than wholegrain flour because the germ, which contains oils that can turn rancid (go off), has been removed.
Improvers (additives that help flour perform when baked) or added nutrients may be incorporated at the end of milling.
Flour is weighed into paper bags. The label gives the brand, product name, ingredients, best-before date, quantity, nutrition information and storage.

Flour is then an ingredient in bread, cakes, pasta and breakfast cereals, each of which passes through further stages such as mixing, baking or extrusion (forcing through a shaped opening), then packaging.
Setting: a visit to a local mill shows these stages in practice.
notes.tip: A profile of flour needs the stages in order, then the packaging and the label contents. Remember the effect of removing the germ: white flour keeps longer than wholemeal.

notes.h: Profile 2: food processed to extend shelf life
notes.b: Milk spoils quickly because micro-organisms and enzymes act on it. Preservation methods slow or stop the micro-organisms and enzymes that spoil food, so milk goes through several treatments at the creamery.
points: A creamery receives milk from farms, tests its quality, cools it, separates cream from skimmed milk, standardises the fat content, pasteurises it, cools it again, packs it and keeps it in chill storage.
Pasteurisation heats milk (to about 72 °C for 15 seconds) to destroy pathogens and most spoilage organisms, then cools it rapidly. The milk still needs refrigeration and keeps for days.

UHT (ultra-high temperature) treatment heats milk to about 135 °C for a few seconds. Sealed in aseptic (germ-free) packaging, it keeps for months at room temperature until opened. Sterilised milk is heated even more severely in the sealed bottle.

Homogenisation forces milk under pressure through tiny openings, breaking fat globules so that cream does not rise to the top. This improves consistency but is not a preservation step and does not kill bacteria.
Canning heats food in sealed containers to destroy micro-organisms; freezing and storage at or below -18 °C stops most micro-organisms from growing.
Drying removes moisture so micro-organisms cannot grow, and vacuum packing removes air to slow spoilage.
Setting: a visit to a local creamery or cheese plant shows milk being pasteurised and separated in practice.
notes.tip: Do not say homogenisation kills bacteria: it stops cream rising and is not preservation. Keep pasteurisation (cool, short life) and UHT (months at room temperature) clearly apart.

notes.b: Added value means processing a raw material into a product with greater economic value, not a more nutritious one. The product is worth more to the manufacturer and is better matched to consumer taste, convenience or health.
points: For example, cook-chill soups and readymade meals, cheese and grated cheese, flavoured yoghurts, sliced cooked ham, herb-flavoured oils and vinegars, jams, pickles and fruit sauces.
Cook-chill foods are cooked, chilled rapidly (to 3 °C within 30 minutes and fully chilled within 90 minutes), stored and transported at 1-3 °C, and reheated thoroughly before serving.
Milk is the raw material for cheese and yoghurt; each involves culturing, coagulating or otherwise changing the milk into a new product with a higher selling price.

Cheese: pasteurised milk is inoculated (given a starter) with lactic acid bacteria, which turn lactose into lactic acid. Rennet coagulates it into curds and whey, the curds are cut and the whey drained, then the curds are heated, cheddared, salted, moulded and pressed.
The cheese is then ripened for months, graded, cut and sealed.
The manufacturer gains a higher selling price, while the consumer gains convenience, taste or a health benefit.
notes.tip: A profile of an added-value food needs the product name, why it is added value, the stages of production, the packaging and the label. Choose cheese, yoghurt or a cook-chill meal, give at least six ordered stages, then the pack (foil, plastic tub, waxed paper) and label contents such as brand, producer, best-before date, nutrition, storage and allergens.

notes.b: Yoghurt is a worked example of added value: ordinary milk is fermented into a thicker, sour product that sells for more. Follow the stages in order.
points: 1. Milk is tested on reception and its fat content is standardised (adjusted to a set level); milk solids may be added to give body.
2. Milk is homogenised under pressure so that fat globules stay evenly dispersed.
3. Milk is pasteurised to destroy pathogens, then cooled to the temperature the starter culture needs.
4. Lactic acid bacteria, and any probiotic culture, are added and the milk is incubated; the bacteria ferment lactose to lactic acid.
5. The falling pH (it becomes more acidic) coagulates the casein (the main milk protein), giving yoghurt its thick texture and sour flavour.
6. Once the correct acidity is reached, the yoghurt is chilled quickly to slow fermentation.

7. Fruit purée, permitted sugar, stabiliser or flavouring may be blended in; the yoghurt is filled, sealed, coded and kept refrigerated in the chill chain (the unbroken cold storage from factory to shop).

notes.b: Some foods are chosen for more than their basic nutrients. A functional food has a health benefit on top of ordinary nutrition.
points: A functional food gives health benefits beyond its basic nutritional value because of an added or naturally present ingredient.
Live yoghurt with probiotic bacteria supports the digestive system, because the added bacteria are the beneficial ingredient.
Plant sterol spreads reduce blood cholesterol, so they are chosen by people wanting to lower it.
Omega-3 enriched foods are promoted for heart health.
Folic acid enriched foods reduce the risk of neural tube defects (birth defects of the brain and spine) in a developing baby.
notes.tip: Explain functional food in two lines with an example: a health benefit beyond nutritive value, such as probiotic yoghurt or plant-sterol spreads. A functional food is not the same as a fortified food, though one product can be both.

notes.b: Fortification is a way of putting nutrients into foods that people eat every day. It is different from food supplements, which are tablets.
points: Fortification adds nutrients so that their level in the food is higher than the level naturally present.
Fortification replaces nutrients lost in processing, so the food is not poorer, and addresses public health needs.
Breakfast cereals are often fortified with iron and vitamins, fruit juices with vitamin C, and margarine and dairy spreads with vitamins A and D.
Other foods named as fortified include milk, flour, bread and biscuits.
notes.tip: If asked to explain the term fortified, say that the nutrient level is raised above what is naturally present, then give the consumer benefit and name fortified foods. Do not confuse fortification with supplements.

notes.h: Merits of processed and convenience foods
notes.b: Convenience foods are processed foods that are ready to eat or quick to prepare. They are popular because they solve real problems for busy households.
points: They save preparation, cooking and cleaning time and need little cooking skill, which suits busy households and people with limited mobility.
Long shelf life gives a wide choice of food all year round, including out-of-season produce.
They give consistent quality, taste and portion size, and clear portions aid meal planning.
Processing reduces waste, so less food is thrown out, and frozen or canned foods keep many of their nutrients.
They are easy to store, so they are useful as an emergency meal.
notes.tip: Exams ask for about four developed points, not a list of single words, and the higher-level question asks for both merits and drawbacks and a balanced judgement. A good judgement is to use processed foods selectively, compare labels and combine them with fresh food.

notes.h: Disadvantages of processed and convenience foods
notes.b: The same foods have drawbacks for health, cost and the environment, which is why they should not make up the whole diet.
points: Many are high in salt, sugar and saturated fat and low in fibre.
They are often more expensive per portion than home-prepared food of similar size, because the maker's processing and packaging costs are added to the price.
Many contain additives, a minority of consumers react to particular substances.
Packaging adds waste and environmental impact.
Reliance on ready meals reduces cooking skills, because meals are no longer made from scratch, and can unbalance the diet.
Taste, colour and texture can be inferior to the fresh equivalent, because heating and storage change them.
notes.tip: When discussing processed foods, give both sides and finish with a balanced judgement rather than only listing drawbacks.

notes.b: Ultra-processed foods are at the far end of processing. They are made in factories from refined ingredients and additives rather than from whole foods.
points: Ultra-processed foods are industrial formulations made largely from refined ingredients and additives, with little or no whole food. They are classed as group 4 in the NOVA system.
Examples, such as packaged snacks, sugary drinks, instant noodles and many ready meals.
They are designed for convenience, palatability (how pleasant they taste) and long shelf life, and often contain flavourings, colourings, emulsifiers and sweeteners that are not used in home cooking.
They are less healthy than fresh food.
notes.tip: A true or false question can ask whether ultra-processed foods are healthier than fresh food: they are less healthy.

notes.b: Two other labels on food describe how it was produced: genetic modification changes the plant or animal itself, while organic farming limits the chemicals used to grow it.
points: Genetic modification alters the DNA of a plant or animal to change a characteristic such as size, speed of ripening or resistance to disease.
Soya and maize are examples of crops widely grown as genetically modified varieties.
EU law requires foods containing genetically modified ingredients, including foods made from genetically modified soya or maize, to be labelled.
Organic produce is grown without synthetic chemical fertilisers, pesticides and preservatives.
Organic farming is less intensive, so it gives lower yields, and must follow rules on fertiliser use and on pest, weed and disease control.
Organic certification is given by inspection bodies recognised by the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, and certified products carry the symbol of the certifying body.
Lower yields and more labour make organic food more expensive.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one-line notes on GM food, organic food or added-value food. For GM food, say the DNA is altered and the food must be labelled; for organic food, say no synthetic fertilisers or pesticides, certified, dearer.

keyTerms.definition: Any food changed from its raw state by one or more processes, such as milling, heating, freezing or adding ingredients.
Processing that involves many stages and ingredients, so the final product is far removed from its raw material.
Heating milk to a set temperature for a set time to destroy pathogens and most spoilage organisms, then cooling it rapidly.
Ultra-high temperature heat treatment for a few seconds, followed by aseptic packaging, which gives milk a long shelf life until opened.
A product made by processing a raw material so that it has greater economic value or better suits consumer needs.
Food that is cooked, rapidly chilled, kept refrigerated and reheated thoroughly before serving.
A food that gives health benefits beyond its basic nutritional value because of an added or naturally present ingredient.
A live micro-organism that, when eaten in sufficient amounts, benefits the digestive system.
Adding nutrients to food so that their level is higher than the level naturally present.
An industrial formulation made largely from refined ingredients and additives, with little or no whole food.
Forcing milk under pressure through small openings so that fat globules are broken up and stay evenly dispersed.
Altering the DNA of an organism to change a characteristic such as size, ripening speed or disease resistance.

It is heated to a very high temperature for a few seconds and sealed in aseptic packaging, so it keeps at room temperature until opened.

questions.prompt: A dairy processor turns surplus milk into a new product that sells for more than raw milk. Explain why this product is an added-value food, and name two examples of added-value foods.
questions.model: An added-value food is made by processing a raw material so that it has greater economic value and better meets consumer needs. Milk is processed into a product with a higher selling price than the raw milk, by adding ingredients or by processes such as culturing, flavouring or cooking. Two examples: cheese or grated cheese; live yoghurt; cook-chill soup; readymade meals; sliced ham; herb-flavoured oils; jams; pickles.

questions.prompt: Discuss the merits and disadvantages of including processed and convenience foods in a busy family's diet, and suggest how the family could use them to best effect.
questions.model: Merits: they save preparation, cooking and cleaning time and need little skill; a long shelf life gives year-round choice; quality and portion size are consistent; little food is wasted; frozen and canned foods keep many nutrients; fortification can add vitamins and minerals; they are easy to store and useful in an emergency. Disadvantages: many are high in salt, sugar and saturated fat and low in fibre; they are often dearer per portion than home cooking; many contain additives, and some consumers react to particular substances; packaging adds waste; reliance on ready meals reduces cooking skills and can unbalance the diet; large portions and marketing can encourage overeating. Use: choose products by comparing labels, keep the portion sizes sensible, and combine them with fresh vegetables, wholegrains and fruit, so that the convenience is used selectively and the diet stays balanced.
